## 1. Identification Strategy  
Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS) difference-in-differences.

• First stage: exploit exogenous variation in IPO completion generated by the 2-month NASDAQ return that is realized **after** the firm has already filed its S-1.  
• Second stage: compare post-filing innovative outcomes of firms that, because of a favorable NASDAQ shock, complete the IPO (“treated”) with those that, because of an unfavorable shock, remain private (“controls”).  
• A pre/post panel with firm fixed effects absorbs all time-invariant differences across firms, so the identifying variation is the interaction of (i) the NASDAQ-driven probability of going public and (ii) within-firm before/after changes in innovation.  

This IV-DID hybrid is appropriate because:  
1. The NASDAQ shock is externally determined and uncorrelated with firm-specific innovation plans.  
2. The patent panel allows observation of each firm before and after the IPO decision, satisfying the parallel-trends component conditional on the instrument.

## 2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
• `IPO_i` = 1 if firm i completes the IPO within 12 months of the S-1 filing; 0 otherwise (withdrawn filings).

Instrument  
• `NASDAQ2m_i` = cumulative log return on the NASDAQ Composite from day +1 to day +60 relative to the firm’s S-1 filing date.

Control group  
• Firms that filed an S-1 in the same calendar quarter but ultimately withdrew, i.e., `IPO_i = 0`.

Treatment timing  
• Event time t = 0 is the S-1 filing date. We define “pre” as patent activity in the (–3, –1] years relative to filing and “post” as (+1, +3] years. Patents filed during the registration/quiet period (0 to +90 days) are dropped to avoid endogenous timing adjustments.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Instrument relevance: NASDAQ2m strongly predicts IPO completion.  
• Plausible; historical withdrawal waves line up with market swings. (First-stage F ≫ 10 expected.)

A2. Exclusion restriction: Conditional on firm and calendar-year fixed effects, NASDAQ2m influences future innovation only through IPO status, not through any direct channel.  
• Plausible because firms cannot trade on the market return realized after filing and the window is short; market returns are absorbed in year FE.

A3. Monotonicity: A higher NASDAQ return weakly increases, never decreases, the probability that any given filer completes its IPO.  
• Consistent with the book-building & pricing process—no firm is forced to withdraw in a rising market.

A4. Parallel trends (for the DID component): In absence of going public, treated and control filers would have followed similar patenting trajectories.  
• Reasonable because they are all IPO‐intending firms with similar filing dates; can be probed with event-study pre-trends.

A5. SUTVA: One firm’s IPO status does not affect another filer’s innovation within the window under study.  
• Likely satisfied; R&D and patenting are largely internal.

## 4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

T1. Selective withdrawal related to unobserved shocks to innovation demand (e.g., product failure) that also correlate with NASDAQ returns.  
 • Include firm×industry×year controls for product market news (e.g., FDA decisions for biotech).  
 • Show balance on pre-filing patent growth and on other real variables by NASDAQ deciles.

T2. Anticipatory changes in patenting while still private (firms may accelerate or delay applications in response to market‐wide signals).  
 • Drop patents applied for in the –90 to +90 day window around filing.  
 • Event-study plots to confirm no differential trend in –3…–1 years.

T3. Instrument manipulation (timing of the S-1 filing). Firms might file when they expect the market to rise.  
 • Use only the portion of NASDAQ return that is orthogonal to returns in the 30 days **before** filing (residualized instrument).  
 • Robustness: restrict to firms that file immediately after SEC reviews, when timing is less discretionary.

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# --- 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dim FE & IV
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# --- 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------------------
pat   <- fread("firm_patents.csv")      # firm-year panel of patent outcomes
ipo   <- fread("ipo_filings.csv")       # S-1 filings incl. outcome + dates
nasd  <- fread("nasdaq_returns.csv")    # daily NASDAQ levels

# --- 2. Construct key variables --------------------------------------------
# 2.1 cumulative NASDAQ return +1 to +60 trading days after filing
nasd[, rtn := log(close) - log(shift(close, type="lag"))]

ipo[, `:=`(start = filing_date + 1,
           end   = filing_date + 60)]
ipo <- merge(ipo,
             nasd[, .(date, rtn)],
             by.x = "start", by.y = "date", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
ipo[, NASDAQ2m := sum(rtn[date >= start & date <= end]), by = .(cik)]

# 2.2 treatment indicator
ipo[, IPO := as.integer(status == "completed")]

# 2.3 merge to patent panel
df <- merge(pat, ipo[, .(cik, filing_date, IPO, NASDAQ2m)], by = "cik")

# 2.4 relative year to filing
df[, rel_year := year - year(filing_date)]
df <- df[rel_year %between% c(-3, 3) & !(rel_year %between% c(0,0))] # drop quiet period

# 2.5 outcome variables
df[, `:=`(pat_total = sum(patent_count),
          cit_per_pat = forward_cites / pmax(1, patent_count)), 
   by = .(cik, year)]

# create post indicator
df[, post := as.integer(rel_year >= 1)]

# --- 3. 2SLS DID specification ---------------------------------------------
# outcome: total patents in post period
iv_formula <- pat_total ~ post*IPO | post*NASDAQ2m + cik + year

est <- feols(iv_formula, data = df, cluster = ~cik)
summary(est)

# --- 4. Robustness: alternative window (30-day NASDAQ return) --------------
ipo[, NASDAQ1m := frollsum(rtn, n = 30)]   # redo code appropriately
df2 <- merge(df, ipo[, .(cik, NASDAQ1m)], by = "cik")
est_rb <- feols(pat_total ~ post*IPO | post*NASDAQ1m + cik + year,
                data = df2, cluster = ~cik)
summary(est_rb)

# --- 5. Pre-trend event study check ----------------------------------------
event <- feols(pat_total ~ i(rel_year, IPO, ref=-1) + cik + filing_cohort, data=df)
iplot(event, ref.line = -0.5)   # should show flat coefficients pre-filing
```

## 6. Expected Results  

Economic theory offers two countervailing forces:  
• Access to public capital can increase R&D spending, boosting patent counts.  
• Short-term market pressure can tilt firms toward incremental, less exploratory research.  

Prior expectation:  
• Quantity: ~20–30 % more patents in the first three post-IPO years.  
• Quality: ~10–15 % decline in forward citations per patent and in originality/generality metrics.  
Hence, total inventive output rises but the **average quality** falls.

## 7. Validity Checklist (IV context)  

C1: Instrument strongly predicts treatment ............... 1  
C2: No direct path from instrument to outcome (exclusion)  0.7  
C3: Monotonicity (NASDAQ ↑ → IPO probability ↑) .......... 1  
C4: Parallel pre-trends (tested via event study) ......... 0.8  
C5: SUTVA / no interference .............................. 1  

Overall self-assessment ≈ 4.5 / 5.
